deeper.title: What the price assumes
deeper.text: The price assumes about 12% a year growth in free cash flow for 10 years, then 3% (discount rate 9.9% = 10-year Treasury 4.9% + 5%; base: last 12 months of free cash flow). For comparison, sales grew 83% last year; 110%/yr over 3 years — the market expects a slowdown from its recent pace.

deeper.title: Return on capital
deeper.text: 81% (3 years ago 47%, rising) — each $100 invested in the business (debt + equity, net of cash) earns about $81 a year after tax; return on shareholders' equity 84% (3 years ago 38%).

deeper.title: Signed future revenue
deeper.text: Signed but not yet delivered (remaining performance obligations): $3.2B, up 68% from a year ago — about 1% of the last 12 months of sales; customer prepayments not yet earned (deferred revenue): $6.4B, up 215% from a year ago.

META (customer): “How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent” → a stronger customer usually means more orders for NVDA.
AI spending: big cloud companies' capital spending is up 88% from a year ago → supports demand for NVDA.
US export controls on advanced chips: “NVIDIA Board of Directors Establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight…”.

connects_more.text: GOOGL (customer): “Intensifying AI rout wipes out Nasdaq's 2026 gains. Alphabet is a tech bright spot” → a stronger customer usually means more orders for NVDA.
ORCL (customer): “Big bets against AI debt, from CoreWeave to Oracle and the Mag 7, could soon hit the ETF…” → a weaker customer can mean fewer orders for NVDA.
NBIS (customer): “Nebius falls 10% as company expects increased 2026 capex spend, issues weak outlook” → its spending plans decide how much it buys from NVDA.
Interest rates: next jobs report on Dec 4 → higher rates weigh most on highly valued stocks.
MU (supplier) reports Dec 17: a read-across for NVDA's supply and costs.
MSFT (customer): Azure is a major buyer of NVIDIA data-center GPUs.
AMZN (customer): AWS is a major buyer of NVIDIA data-center GPUs.
AMD (rival): Both 10-Ks name each other as competitors in GPUs/accelerators.
CRWV (customer): CoreWeave S-1 describes dependence on NVIDIA GPUs; NVIDIA is also an investor.
SMCI (customer): Supermicro builds NVIDIA GPU servers; depends on GPU allocation.
VRT (partner): Vertiv and NVIDIA announced joint data-center power/cooling reference designs.
DELL (customer): Dell AI servers built on NVIDIA GPUs.
INTC (rival): Intel named as a competitor in NVIDIA 10-K.
ASML (affects NVDA): ASML lithography sets leading-edge capacity at TSMC, which builds NVIDIA's GPUs (indirect).
TSLA (customer): Tesla trains its driving models on large NVIDIA GPU clusters (reported).

note.headline: NVIDIA drops 5.86% to 155.38 as Huang comeback rally fades; still hold

summary.thesis: NVIDIA's cash generation is exceptional, and today's price already assumes free cash flow starts growing at about 20% a year. The upside depends on a record 65% operating margin holding.
summary.decision: Hold the long-term position and make no swing trade while the price sits between support and resistance in a downtrend.
summary.act_at: Buy at 116.97, move to wait on a close below 147.14, trim near 222.58

note.happening: NVIDIA fell 5.86% to 155.38, giving back part of the rally that followed Jensen Huang's reported return as CEO. Headlines today are mostly about governance: the government's role in his return, open investigations, and a reported addition of Megaspeed to the U.S. trade blacklist over export controls. Our data has no earnings date, and the latest filed quarter ended 2026-07-26.
note.business: The business numbers are strong. Over the last twelve months revenue was 303.0B, up from 165.2B. Free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) was 127.0B, up from 72.0B. Operating margin rose to 65.21% from 58.09%, and the company holds 23.2B more cash than debt. None of today's CEO news changes these figures. The leadership drama, the investigations and Huang reportedly saying he still does not believe in succession planning affect sentiment and governance, not demand. Two items could touch the business. First, the Megaspeed blacklisting (reported) concerns export controls, which can limit where chips are sold (general knowledge). Second, Amazon's reported Decart deal is a bet on narrowing the chip gap with NVIDIA, a long-run competition risk. The real risks come from the filings. The 65% margin sits at the top of its 5-year range of 16–65%, and peaks like that usually fade. Money customers still owe is up 127% while quarterly sales are up 106%, which can mean sales were pulled forward or customers are stretched. Demand itself does not look at risk today. What is at risk is how long the margin and the payment timing hold.

worth.text: The two methods disagree mainly because they make different assumptions about growth. A discounted cash flow model values the company from its expected future cash. Using the 127.0B in trailing free cash flow and a discount rate near 10%, it gives 191.49 (bear), 222.58 (base) and 264.22 (bull). The company's own price-to-sales history gives 217.35 to 411.04. The more useful reading runs the other way. At 155.38, the price matches the model value of 155.64, which is what 20% starting growth produces, and the data puts the implied starting growth at 20.0%. So the market is not paying for the 83% sales growth of last year. It is paying for growth to slow sharply. The biggest swing factor is margin. If operating margin falls to 48%, the value drops to 116.97, and at 32% it drops to 78.3. The data's valuation summary quotes an older price of 165.05, so today's price sits even lower against those ranges. Multiples tell the same story: 19.6 times trailing earnings, 9.4 times next year's expected earnings, and 12.4 times sales against a peer median of 14.9.
worth.key_assumption: Operating margin stays near 65.21% rather than fading toward 48%, while free cash flow grows from 127.0B at a starting rate of about 20% or more.
